  no one will ring until spring.
  Cars sit under soft mounds,
  their shapes kept only as rumors.

  Nothing here asks permission.
  It arrives without a sound you can name,
  a hush that spreads from the sky downward
  until the ground is a page
  no one has yet written on.

  Look closely at one flake
  and it is a small engineering miracle,
  six arms branching from a single seed,
  each arm grown in its own weather,
  no two alike, none of them remembered
  once they touch the glove on your hand
  and become, briefly, water again.

  A child stands at the window
  counting. He gets to forty
  and loses track, which is the point.
  Snow is the only thing that makes
  a whole city stop doing arithmetic.

  Down the block the plow passes
  like a slow argument with the street,
  pushing the white into black ridges
  that will harden by morning into ice
  and blame. Salt goes down after,
  gray grit scattered like pepper,
  and the neighbors nod at each other
  across their shoveled squares of concrete,
  two strangers bound by
